item.title: Jensen Huang’s Nvidia return buoys South Korea, Japan stocks
item.description: Japanese and South Korean stocks surged in early trade on Tuesday, tracking big gains on Wall Street after the shock reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The benchmark Kospi was up 338.61 points, or 7.19 per cent, at 5,047.15 on Tuesday morning after gains triggered a five-minute “sidecar” curb on programme trading. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was up 3.88 per cent at 58,623.73 points. In overnight trade, shares of Nvidia rose more than 30 per cent on Huang’s reinstatement as CEO in a stunning...

item.title: Hong Kong’s Wang Fuk Court fire victims to receive new cash grant of up to HK$300,000
item.description: Victims of the Wang Fuk Court fire will receive a new cash grant of up to HK$300,000, the Hong Kong government has announced two days ahead of the first anniversary of the blaze, as the city’s No 2 official pledged a “resident-oriented” approach to reforms. Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki said on Tuesday that the government would implement all 120 recommendations by the independent committee that investigated the city’s deadliest fire in decades, with nearly 90 per cent of the proposals...

item.title: ‘Eternal hometown’: US man, 95, donates medical devices to small Chinese town over 2 decades
item.description: A 95-year-old American man has donated medical equipment worth more than six million yuan (US$900,000) to a small, remote county in northwestern China with which he has a lifelong bond. China’s foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning praised David V. Plymire in October as an example of people-to-people communication. item.title: Billionaire Richard Li shares guitar playing on social media, sparking slew of reactions
item.description: Billionaire Richard Li Tzar-kai, the second son of Hong Kong’s richest man Li Ka-shing, has apparently posted videos of himself on Instagram playing the guitar, including a song by Taiwanese singer Eric Chou, drawing a flurry of reactions from surprised internet users. item.title: China’s historical climate records could be skewed by human bias, study finds
item.description: For centuries, scholars, officials and local chroniclers in China recorded the world around them, resulting in a collection of imperial histories, gazetteers, personal diaries and records that is seen as the most continuous in the world. Among them are detailed accounts of the weather – including droughts, floods and harvest conditions – which researchers have used to try to reconstruct and understand the region’s climate history.
